Bootlin's embedded Linux course runs 5 days / 40 hours on site or 7 half days / 28 hours online; all its training materials are freely available; it expects command-line familiarity and points beginners to Bootlin's free command-line slides
The Linux Foundation's Introduction to Linux (LFS101) is listed as a free training course covering the graphical interface and command line across the major distribution families

The online 'stable' edition of The Debian Administrator's Handbook covers Debian 11 Bullseye ('Debian Bullseye from Discovery to Mastery'), dual-licensed CC BY-SA 3.0 and GPL-2.0-or-later [so it predates Debian 13 trixie by two releases]

Linux From Scratch provides step-by-step instructions to build a customized Linux system entirely from source; the SysV book is no longer maintained and the systemd book is the maintained line [current version number inferred as 13.1 from a translation link; not stated directly on the page]

The kernel's PREEMPT_RT documentation (core-api/real-time) is written for kernel developers and covers theory of operation (sleeping spin locks, priority inheritance, threaded interrupts), how RT kernels differ, hardware considerations, porting an architecture and RT kernel configuration
systemd-cryptenroll enrolls PKCS#11 tokens, FIDO2 security keys, TPM2 devices and randomly generated recovery keys (which can be scanned as QR codes) on LUKS2 volumes
The UAPI Group publishes the Boot Loader Specification (UAPI.1), the Discoverable Partitions Specification (UAPI.2), Discoverable Disk Images (UAPI.3) and Unified Kernel Images (UAPI.5)

RAUC integration: system.conf is read from the first of /etc/rauc, /run/rauc, /usr/lib/rauc; it sets a compatible string, the bootloader backend and [slot.<class>.<index>] entries; the target needs a keyring (default ca.cert.pem) and the build host a signing key and certificate as PEM files or PKCS#11 URIs (e.g. an HSM); backends are grub, efi and custom (handler with get-primary/set-primary/get-state/set-state)

RAUC's efi backend uses the BootCurrent EFI variable to find the booted entry and map it to a slot; the documented layout is two redundant VFAT partitions holding EFI-stub kernels or UKIs, each the parent of a rootfs slot; RAUC's docs say the ESP type GUID can be omitted on those partitions so firmware does not auto-create or update boot entries that interfere with RAUC-managed A/B entries [this differs from 01 §4.3, which gives boot-a/b the ESP type and relies on SB-2 entry clean-up; flagged for W3]

Raspberry Pi firmware 'tryboot': a one-shot flag set with `reboot '0 tryboot'` loads tryboot.txt (or, with secure boot, tryboot.img) once and is then cleared; with tryboot_a_b=1 in autoboot.txt the switch happens at partition level; all Raspberry Pi models support it
Docker's multi-platform build guide describes three strategies: QEMU emulation, multiple native builder nodes, and cross-compilation

k3s architecture: a server node runs `k3s server` with control-plane and datastore components; an agent node runs `k3s agent` with no datastore or control-plane components; both run the kubelet, container runtime and CNI; the single-server setup uses an embedded database

k3s docs: 'No special commands are required to back up or restore the SQLite datastore' (copy /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/); the server token file must also be backed up and restored or passed with --token, because the token encrypts confidential data and a different token makes the snapshot unusable [OneMind hardens this with an online sqlite3 .backup, see C-W5-009]
The k3s docs carry a CIS Hardening Guide plus CIS self-assessment guides for benchmarks 2.0, 1.12 and 1.11
Kubernetes The Hard Way is 'optimized for learning' (it takes the long route through each step) and its results 'should not be viewed as production ready'

NATS docs: a leaf node is a NATS server that opens an outbound connection to a remote NATS system and bridges subject interest; local clients need no leaf-specific config; a leaf can bind to a named account that decides which subjects cross; a leaf running its own JetStream needs a distinct JetStream domain or the two JetStream systems can collide
NATS docs cover authentication by password, token, bearer JWT, mTLS or NKey signatures, accounts and multitenancy, operator mode, decentralized (JWT) authentication and auth callout

NATS by Example is 'an evolving collection of runnable, cross-client reference examples for NATS', including JetStream, KV, object store, NKeys/JWT auth and leaf-node topologies (including leaf nodes with JWT auth) [maintainer not stated on the page]
The SLSA v1.1 specification page states that Version 1.2 is the current version
Sigstore's documentation covers Cosign (signing, keyless signing quickstart) and the Rekor transparency log

'A Practical Guide to TPM 2.0' (Will Arthur and David Challener, Apress, 2015) is an ApressOpen open-access book (free, noncommercial use) [Springer's page redirected to a login/bot check; open-access status taken from search results and the DOAB listing, not opened]
